title: After-School Care Inside Senior Living Communities
one_liner: Turn senior living's empty afternoon dining rooms into licensed school-age programs where residents are reading, repair and garden 'buddies', funded by parent tuition, operator economics and loneliness-intervention budgets.
customer: Working parents of K-5 kids near independent- and assisted-living communities (dependent-care FSA eligible, cap $7,500). Secondary payers: senior living operators seeking occupancy and retention, and Medicare Advantage plans or Area Agencies on Aging funding loneliness programs.
problem: The 3-6pm care gap is where parents lose work hours, and average US childcare costs $13,128 (35% of income for single parents). Older adults are the least-served, highest-need loneliness segment, and 40-46% of adults 65+ are 'unsure' about AI companions (Pew, Aug 2026), so a human alternative has open ground. Operators have empty spaces between lunch and dinner and no scalable, reimbursable engagement model.
solution: 'Bridge Clubs': the community lends the room 2:30-6pm. We run a licensed school-age program (1:12 ratio, bus drop from the elementary school). Residents opt into structured 30-minute roles ('Reading Elders', 'Tinkerers', 'Garden Crew'). We track participation and a loneliness scale (UCLA-3) monthly and package the data for MA plans and AAAs so they can fund resident engagement. Parents pay less than typical after-school rates because space and volunteer time subsidize it.
why_now: The dependent-care FSA cap rose to $7,500 and the 45F employer childcare credit rose to 40% (50% for small businesses) in 2026, opening employer and parent budgets. WHO's 2025 Commission put loneliness on the health agenda. Payers are hunting for measurable loneliness interventions, and school-age licensing is lighter than infant care in many states.
revenue_model: Parent tuition of about $325-475/mo. Operator rent-share or management fee. Engagement-based fees from MA plans or AAAs. Employer sponsorship of slots via the 45F credit.
non_obvious_insight: This is two 'deserts' each holding the other's unused capacity. 'Intergenerational programming' usually fails as charity. It works when the payer stack (tuition, operator occupancy, and loneliness reimbursement) makes it profitable and the resident role is a job, not a photo op.
first_30_days: Find three independent-living operators within a mile of Title I elementary schools with after-school waitlists. Run a 6-week pilot with 12 kids in one dining room using a licensed partner provider. Charge $99 registration plus $349/mo. Collect resident participation and UCLA-3 scores. Take the data to one regional MA plan's community benefits team.

title: Bulk Records-Request Refinery, Septic-First
one_liner: Build datasets that do not exist by filing thousands of automated public-records requests to county health departments, then reading the scans with vision models and selling address-level reports.
customer: Home inspectors, buyer's agents, title and closing attorneys, and mortgage lenders and insurers in septic- and well-heavy markets, who pay per address report or a monthly subscription. Later customers are insurers and lenders buying bulk address-level datasets.
problem: About one in five US homes runs on septic and millions rely on private wells. Permits, inspections, pump-outs, repair and abandonment records sit in more than 3,000 county and town health departments, in paper, scans and idiosyncratic portals. There is no national database. Buyers sign blind and face 15-50k USD failed-system replacements. Inspectors and agents make phone calls to find records, or skip the check.
solution: A records-request engine. It knows each state's open-records statute, fee categories and portal type. It bulk-files requests, tracks deadlines, and follows up. A vision-language pipeline reads handwritten and scanned forms, extracts fields (install date, tank size, drainfield type, repairs, failed inspections, well depth and tests) and geocodes them to parcels. Sell address-level reports for 39-99 USD, with a guarantee of retrieve or refund at first. Every answered request becomes a permanent proprietary data asset, so the data compounds. The same engine expands to other records with no national database: hydrant flow tests, fire inspections, certificates of occupancy, unpermitted-work flags, underground tanks and radon.
why_now: Vision-language models now read messy handwriting and scanned forms at fractions of a cent per page, which made this economically impossible until recently. Most jurisdictions have moved to online request portals, making bulk filing feasible without postage and paper. Agents can draft statute-specific requests and chase deadlines automatically. Home-inspection firms are looking for differentiated services in a slow transaction market.
revenue_model: Pay-per-address report (39-99 USD), inspector subscriptions (149-399 USD per month for unlimited lookups in their region), and enterprise data licenses to insurers and lenders. Later, sell the engine as a service to other data-hungry industries that need one specific municipal record type at national scale.
non_obvious_insight: Government data is not secret, just expensive to collect, and that friction is the moat. Every request is legal, cheap and repeatable, but nobody wants to make 3,000 of them by hand, so once you have, nobody can scrape or replicate your dataset from the web. Concierge fulfillment lets you get paid on day one before the automation exists, and every manual retrieval trains the pipeline.
first_30_days: Choose one state with a septic-heavy housing stock and a friendly open-records law (for example, a state where county health departments handle onsite wastewater, such as North Carolina). Check the state law for commercial-requester restrictions and fee schedules. Offer 20 local home inspectors a 75 USD 'we retrieve the septic record or refund you' service, fulfilled manually or semi-manually at first. Simultaneously file bulk requests to every county health department for historical records. Run the vision extraction pipeline on the first few thousand pages, and use the results to pitch a subscription to inspector networks and title companies.

title: Half-Pro Remodeling: Homeowner Does the Easy 60%
one_liner: Fixed-price booking of only the licensed, permit-required slice of a project while homeowners or handymen do demo, prep and finish, with photo-verified handoffs.
customer: Budget-constrained homeowners with $3-15K bath, kitchen, water-heater, mini-split and electrical projects. Supply side: solo licensed plumbers and electricians who want prequalified, ready-to-work half-day jobs.
problem: Angi data shows 73% of homeowners have unstarted projects and 72% of postponers cite budget. The average project is $5,368. DIY-only fell from 50% to 39% while homeowner-plus-pro rose from 27% to 46%. Pros say they are too busy and skip small, messy, scope-uncertain jobs. Platforms sell whole jobs, so homeowners get no quotes.
solution: A catalog of standardized pro steps: rough-in for a vanity swap, shutoff valve and supply lines, gas line, water heater swap, ceiling-fan or lighting circuit, mini-split hookup, permit pull and inspection sign-off. Each comes with a homeowner checklist (nine prep steps, three photos) checked by a vision model, and a pro shows up for a fixed price to a job that is actually ready. Start only where owner-builder and licensing rules are clear.
why_now: Angi's 2026 backlog data. Credit cards rose to 30% of project payments. 62% now choose repair over replace. Contractors are capacity-constrained. Multimodal models can verify prep photos cheaply.
revenue_model: 15-20% take on the pro-step price ($300-1,500), plus materials affiliate margin from a local supply house. Pros pay nothing upfront.
non_obvious_insight: The unit of demand is not the project, it is the licensed hour. The blended-work data says homeowners do not want turnkey, they want to transfer risk only on the parts they legally or practically cannot do. Nobody sells the licensed two hours with a photo-checked handoff, and small pros love the productivity of arriving at a ready job.
first_30_days: One metro, four job types. Recruit 10 solo plumbers and electricians from local trade Facebook groups. Launch a landing page with local ads. Run 30 bookings by hand with a spreadsheet and Stripe.

title: Knowledge Trusts That Pay Heirs From AI Licensing
one_liner: A fiduciary licensing shop that records a retiring or terminally ill master practitioner's judgment, holds the rights in an estate-friendly trust, sells non-exclusive licenses to AI buyers, and pays royalties to the expert and later the heirs.
customer: Two payers. First, employers and trade associations with an irreplaceable expert aged 62-75 about to retire, who pay for a knowledge-capture sprint. Second, AI labs, vertical AI vendors and professional-training firms that license the corpus. Beneficiaries are the expert and heirs. Channel: estate attorneys and wealth managers, who want an heir-engagement hook (Cerulli says 89% of firms treat family meetings as essential).
problem: The scarcest input for AI is long-tail, high-stakes tacit judgment (how a 40-year surety underwriter smells a bad bond, how a master electrician diagnoses an odd fault). It sits in the heads of people near retirement or death. Hourly expert-gig marketplaces pay by the hour with no royalties. They rarely reach 65+ specialists, and nobody structures who owns the recordings, annotations or persona rights after death, so it all falls into probate limbo. Meanwhile 22-25-year-olds in AI-exposed jobs are about 19% below trend (Stanford) and have no path to learn from these people.
solution: 1) Structured elicitation: 30-40 hours of rubric-guided sessions (case walk-throughs, 'what would you do and why not that', annotated redacted real work). Junior apprentice-interviewers from the same field, meaning recent grads or displaced mid-career people, run them. They are paid and earn a verifiable co-credit. 2) Rights go into a knowledge trust drafted with the client's estate attorney: consent controls, approved-buyer list, sunset dates, and no voice, likeness or persona cloning unless explicitly opted in. 3) Non-exclusive licensing of the corpus to labs and enterprise vendors. Royalties go to the expert while alive and to heirs afterward.
why_now: Mercor's $10B valuation (Oct 2025) and reported ~$2B gross run-rate (Jun 2026, lower-tier source, verify) proved frontier labs pay heavily for expert judgment, while contractors complain about pay and lack of protection. Roughly 4M Americans turn 65 each year, and Cerulli projects $124T in transfers through 2048. Postmortem publicity and digital-replica laws are maturing (for example California's 70-year postmortem term). The junior hiring freeze creates a cheap, motivated interviewer pool.
revenue_model: Employer-funded capture sprints at $15-40K per expert (a succession-planning budget line). License revenue share, roughly 40% to expert/estate, 40% to us, 20% to an apprentice pool. Trust administration fee of about 1% of royalties per year. Optional per-client fee from advisors or attorneys who bundle it into estate plans.
non_obvious_insight: The estate, not the living person, is the natural licensor of a lifetime of judgment. Postmortem and IP rights live in probate, and royalty streams fit inheritance planning better than hourly gigs do. Retirees who would never take a gig will happily fund grandchildren with a legacy asset. The demand is a fixed-time resource (a retirement wave) that becomes unavailable once experts are gone.
first_30_days: Pick two narrow, lab-relevant, high-liability trades (for example construction surety adjusters and commercial roofing estimators). Recruit 8-10 retiring experts via trade-association newsletters and five friendly estate attorneys. Pitch each expert's employer a $20K 'retirement capture sprint' as the cash-generating wedge, with licensing rights reserved for the expert's trust. Hire 3 laid-off or junior domain grads as interviewers. Run two pilots. Send redacted sample corpora to 10 human-data teams and vertical AI startups to pre-sell licenses.

title: Tender-Time Snapshots: Post-Montgomery Broker Defense File
one_liner: A tamper-evident, per-load record of exactly what a broker knew about a carrier at the moment of tender, built to survive plaintiff discovery and to satisfy underwriters, then upgraded into a placed contingent-liability program for small brokers.
customer: Independent brokerages and host-agency networks doing roughly $2M-$60M in gross revenue that buy contingent auto liability through a wholesaler. Secondary payers: MGAs, wholesalers and E&S carriers that now need underwriting evidence.
problem: On May 14, 2026 the Supreme Court unanimously held in Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II that negligent-hiring claims against brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA, so state-law suits now reach discovery. Insurance trade press (The Insurer, Sept 17, 2026, quoting RPS) is already calling it a capacity problem for broker contingent liability, and underwriters are asking for a paper trail of what was reviewed, when, and what was concluded. A small broker's carrier file is an onboarding PDF from 14 months ago plus email threads. Authority status, insurance, safety rating, ownership and contact info can change any day, and nobody can show what the screen said on the day of the load.
solution: Hook into tender events (TMS export, rate-con email forward, or load-board booking). At each tender, pull and hash-timestamp a snapshot: authority status, safety rating, insurance certificate validity, CSA/out-of-service rates, recent MCS-150 or contact-info changes, fraud flags, and which of the broker's own written selection rules the carrier passed. Any override is logged with a reason and the person who made it. A one-click 'selection file' export is formatted for a discovery request. Ship templates for a written carrier-selection standard drafted with trucking defense counsel. Phase 2: use the aggregated data to place small brokers into a wholesaler/MGA contingent-liability program with pricing credit for documented behavior.
why_now: Montgomery (May 14, 2026) removed the broad preemption defense. Contingent auto liability and E&O are repricing and capacity is tightening, per industry reporting in Sept 2026. The FMCSA broker financial-responsibility rule took full effect Jan 16, 2026, with suspension if security stays below $75K for 7 business days, so brokers cannot absorb a surprise verdict or claim.
revenue_model: SaaS at $0.50-$1.50 per tendered load or $300-$1,200/month by volume. Phase 2 adds a 10-15% commission on premium placed through the program, plus referral fees from defense firms.
non_obvious_insight: Plaintiffs' counsel does not ask 'did you vet the carrier?' They ask 'show me what your system showed at the minute you tendered, and who overrode it.' Brokers who vetted diligently at onboarding still lose, because they cannot prove tender-day state. Every broker knows the overrides happen at 4:45pm on a Friday when a load must be covered, and underwriters will price that override discipline. The record also proves the absence of red flags, which is the reasonable-care defense.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 small brokers through freight-broker Facebook groups and TIA chapters. Co-write a reasonable-care checklist with one trucking defense attorney. Build a snapshot logger on public FMCSA data plus an insurance-certificate check, ingesting tenders by CSV or forwarded rate-con emails so no TMS integration is needed. The sales hook is a free 'Discovery Fire Drill': simulate a plaintiff's request against the broker's last 5 loads and show the gaps. Convert at $299/month. In parallel, take the aggregate data to two wholesale brokers to test whether a premium credit is feasible.

title: Death Certificate Sign-Off Copilot for Hospices
one_liner: Get physicians to complete valid cause-of-death certifications in hours instead of days, sold to the hospices and care groups that get blamed for the delay, with funeral homes as the free wedge.
customer: Hospice organizations and nursing-home or assisted-living groups. The buyer is the VP of operations or hospice medical director, motivated by family-experience scores and clinician time. Funeral homes use a free version that seeds the data.
problem: Nothing moves until a physician completes the medical section of the death certificate in the state's electronic system. Cremation authorization, burial permits and certified copies for the family all wait. Doctors forget logins, delegate poorly, or enter invalid cause-of-death chains such as 'cardiac arrest', which triggers rejections or medical examiner referrals. A funeral director spends hours per case chasing certifiers, families see the delay as the funeral home's fault, and the cooler fills up while everyone waits.
solution: Phase one is a free web and text tool for funeral homes. They log each pending certificate, and the tool sends the certifier a one-tap reminder with clear instructions and shows a status page. Phase two is the paid hospice product: from the discharge summary or chart export, an AI drafts the Part I/Part II cause-of-death chain in line with NCHS conventions, flags ME-reportable triggers before submission, and routes a mobile magic-link for physician review. In states that allow certifier designees, hospice staff do the data entry. A dashboard shows time-to-certify by physician and site, with escalation rules.
why_now: Electronic death registration systems are now near-universal, so a digital workflow is possible. LLMs can reliably summarize a chart for physician review in a way that wasn't safe or cheap a few years ago. Hospice growth and public CAHPS Hospice scores raise the stakes of family experience. Medical director workloads are rising with physician shortages.
revenue_model: $35-$60 per certificate processed, or $200-$500/month per hospice site plus per-certifier seats. Optional $99/month funeral-home tier with analytics and multi-hospice benchmarking. Later, sell the anonymized time-to-certify benchmark to hospice chains and payers.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone blames the funeral home for slowness, but we spend more time chasing doctors than doing the actual work. This 'post-death workflow orphan' sits after the patient leaves the EHR workflow, so no health-tech vendor sees it. The funeral home is the only party who measures days-from-death-to-certificate. So sell backwards: give funeral homes a free chase tool, collect the scorecard on which hospices and doctors are slow, then walk into those hospices with their own numbers.
first_30_days: Build the no-PHI funeral-home chase tool (case ID, certifier name and phone, state) in two weeks. Recruit 15 funeral homes in two states through the state association. After 60 days publish an anonymized 'days-to-certify by hospice' scorecard. Book meetings with the three slowest hospices and offer a $2,000/month pilot with a signed BAA. Have a physician advisor review the cause-of-death logic.

title: Rural Vet Call Logs as Outbreak Early Warning
one_liner: Producers call the vet before they call the state. Anonymized weekly counts of abortions, maggot wounds, sudden deaths and respiratory clusters are a leading indicator that traders, insurers and packers will pay for.
customer: Buyers: cattle and feeder analytics desks, market advisory and commodity funds, packer and feedlot risk managers, livestock and dairy insurers or reinsurers, animal health company territory teams, and state animal health boards (contracts or grants). Suppliers are participating rural vets, who get free early regional alerts and a small revenue share.
problem: Official disease data lags by weeks because it waits on lab confirmation, and ranchers hesitate to report to the state because a quarantine costs them money. Screwworm was confirmed in a Texas calf in June 2026 after roughly 60 years without a US case, and H5N1 in dairy cattle was spreading for months before detection in 2024. Cattle futures at record prices with a 70-year low herd move violently on rumor, and nobody has a systematic ground-level feed.
solution: A 30-second end-of-week SMS or one-tap tally where each vet reports counts by syndrome (abortion clusters, navel or wound maggots, sudden deaths, neurological, respiratory, milk drops) and ZIP3 or county. Counts are aggregated with k-anonymity (no client identity, minimum practice thresholds) and compared to seasonal baselines. Outputs are a weekly 'Rural Vet Pulse' regional index, push alerts when a region deviates, and an API for institutional subscribers. Vets get the regional alerts free, which is the give-to-get hook.
why_now: New World screwworm has been confirmed in Texas and New Mexico since June 2026, with the first infested horse reported in September 2026, and movement restrictions plus sterile-fly shortages make the outbreak's trajectory the biggest driver of cattle risk. H5N1 in dairy is ongoing, federal animal health staffing is stretched, and academic syndromic surveillance systems exist in Europe (Netherlands, France, Great Britain) but I found no commercial equivalent built from US rural vet practices.
revenue_model: $2-10K per month per institutional data subscriber (analytics desks, insurers, packers), enterprise API tiers, sponsored regional alerts from animal health companies, state or regional government pilots, and a $100-300 per month revenue share to each contributing practice.
non_obvious_insight: Ranchers under-report to the state because reporting costs them money, but they do not hide problems from their vet because they need the vet's drugs and help. The vet's phone is the earliest sensor in the system, and vets cannot share client data but can share counts. Contrarian point: the absence of calls is also a signal, because call volume drops when producers hide problems during a quarantine.
first_30_days: Recruit 25 large-animal practices in Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico, Kansas and Nebraska through state VMA lists and large-animal vet Facebook groups. Build the weekly tally as a plain SMS survey, with no software integration. Publish a free regional weekly newsletter to the vets as the hook. Backtest screwworm lead time against USDA confirmation dates and pitch 3 market-advisory or cattle analytics shops for a $1-2K per month paid pilot.

title: Ex-Botter Red Team for Limited Drops
one_liner: Pay former sneaker-bot users to attack your product drop before launch, then rent you the checkout filter that stops what they found.
customer: Indie brands that run limited drops on Shopify with 500 to 5,000 units: streetwear labels, collectible toy and art-toy makers, TCG shops, sneaker boutiques, merch stores, small beauty and food brands. They pay $750 to $2,500 per pentest, then a per-drop or monthly fee.
problem: Brands think a waiting room or Cloudflare stops scalpers. It only stops speed. Real resellers win by multiplying identities, not by being fast. They use Gmail dot and plus tricks and catch-all domains, address jigging (Apt vs Unit vs #, an extra letter in the street name), virtual cards from one issuer, and residential proxies. One 'customer' becomes 40 orders. Fans get nothing, the brand gets angry DMs, and the resale premium goes to strangers. Small brands cannot afford enterprise bot vendors and do not know what to look for.
solution: Wedge: a 'Drop Pentest'. We run a real reseller stack against the brand's store or staging a week before launch and hand back a report: 'we would have captured 38% of your units, here is how'. Product: a Shopify checkout app called One Per Human. It normalizes emails, fuzzy-dedupes addresses (USPS-style standardization plus apartment and unit variants), clusters card fingerprints and BINs, phone-verifies and blocks VoIP numbers, and flags or auto-cancels suspected multiples before fulfillment, with a human review queue. Optional 'verified reseller tier' at a higher price so the brand captures some of the flip premium legitimately.
why_now: Collectible drops have become a public mess in 2025-26: Labubu and other Pop Mart drops, and Pokemon TCG releases where stores had fights, lines, and pulled product. Indie brands now copy sneaker-style drops, with sneaker-style bot pressure. Cheap LLM fuzzy matching makes address and identity dedupe far cheaper to build than it was two years ago. Shopify's checkout extensibility gives apps a place to validate or flag orders.
revenue_model: Pentest at $750 to $2,500. Guard app at $149 to $499 per drop, or 0.5% to 1% of drop GMV. Annual contracts for brands that drop monthly.
non_obvious_insight: Bots do not beat drops on speed. They beat them on identity multiplication, and the tells sit in the order data (address shape, email pattern, card issuer clusters) that the brand already has. Only someone who has run the tricks knows which tells matter. The poacher-turned-gamekeeper credibility is the moat, and the pentest report sells the product by showing the brand its own leak.
first_30_days: Days 1 to 7: build the attack checklist from what I and my Discord friends already do. Days 7 to 14: DM 100 small Shopify brands with an upcoming drop on Instagram, offering a free mini-audit built from their public store, such as how easy it is to create fake variants of an address. Days 14 to 30: convert 3 to 5 into paid pentests at $750 and use the findings to pre-sell the app. Delivery is mostly a spreadsheet plus screenshots.

title: Short-Time Compensation as a Service
one_liner: Software and admin that lets employers shrink hours instead of headcount using state work-sharing programs, where unemployment insurance replaces part of the lost wages, as an alternative to AI-driven layoffs.
customer: HR and finance leaders at 50-2,000-employee firms in states with work-sharing programs (about half of US states, verify) planning 10-30% reductions in AI-exposed teams. PEOs and payroll providers are channels.
problem: Employers treat headcount cuts as binary, yet many states pay prorated UI when firms cut hours 10-60% rather than lay people off. Almost nobody uses it. AI-driven demand shifts are gradual and uncertain, layoffs risk rehire regret and severance costs, and workers lose health coverage and face 6-13 month searches.
solution: (1) A calculator comparing work-sharing to layoff, including severance, recruiting and regret costs. (2) Plan-filing automation per state. (3) Weekly claim administration integrated with payroll. (4) A training-hours module for reduced-hours periods. (5) Tracking of approvals and caps. (6) A glide path to natural attrition.
why_now: AI restructuring is happening under uncertainty (Challenger shows AI-cited cuts small and partly narrative), reversal headlines are growing, and the market is low-fire, low-hire, so retaining talent has become valuable.
revenue_model: $25-60 per participating employee per month, or 5-10% of validated avoided severance and rehire cost, plus PEO reseller revenue.
non_obvious_insight: The subsidy already exists and is unused because nobody owns the admin burden. Becoming the 'TurboTax for work-sharing' turns a public benefit into a retention and anti-regret hedge that contradicts the 'cut now' reflex.
first_30_days: Map work-sharing rules and forms in the 6-8 biggest states. Interview 15 mid-size HR leads and 5 PEOs. Offer free feasibility analyses to companies that filed WARN notices and convert 2-3 to paid pilots.

title: Kennel Canary: Outbreak Surveillance for Dog Daycares
one_liner: Monthly environmental PCR swabs that give dog daycares, boarders and shelters an early-warning system and proof of due diligence.
customer: Dog daycare, boarding, grooming and training facilities (independents and franchise systems), animal shelters, and the specialty insurers that cover pet-care businesses.
problem: Canine influenza, kennel-cough pathogens and parvo outbreaks force closures, trigger owner lawsuits and tarnish reputation, and a facility can lose 20-30% of a month's revenue in one event. Facilities rely on vaccination records and owner honesty, and testing individual dogs means a vet visit ($150-300) after symptoms appear, which is hard when vets are scarce and 85% of clients decline care above $1,000.
solution: Subscription sentinel kits: pooled air-filter and surface swabs shipped to a partner lab that runs automated multiplex qPCR (CIV, CPIV, CRCoV, Bordetella, Mycoplasma cynos, Strep zooepidemicus, parvo, distemper) with 24-48 hour turnaround. Facilities get a traffic-light dashboard, outbreak playbooks (isolate, sanitize, boost vaccination), and a 'verified-clean' badge for marketing. Insurers receive premium-credit pilots. Aggregated data becomes a regional canine disease early-warning map.
why_now: Post-COVID pet ownership and return-to-office have grown daycare and boarding. Human wastewater and airborne surveillance have matured, and automated extraction plus multiplex PCR have driven per-sample costs down. Regional canine flu and respiratory outbreaks recur, and clinics have less capacity to triage.
revenue_model: $149 per month for a small facility (bi-weekly swabs), $399 per month for multi-room sites, and $50-150k per year for franchise systems. Sample cost is $20-30 at scale. Insurer-paid pilots per insured location and a $10-30k per year data subscription for vaccine makers and veterinary groups.
non_obvious_insight: What these buyers purchase is liability and reputation protection, not health testing. A sentinel result is a dated due-diligence log that insurers and lawyers value, and one avoided closure pays for a year. Pathogen surveillance built for airports and cities has never been priced for the roughly 100,000-plus US pet-care sites.
first_30_days: Partner with a university or commercial vet diagnostic lab that already has a validated respiratory multiplex PCR. Sign 5 daycares via one franchise owner or local trade group for an 8-week pilot at $99 per month. Interview two specialty insurers about credits. Publish a short 'what we found in the air' report to generate inbound interest.

title: Disordered-Eating Tripwire for GLP-1 Prescribers
one_liner: A cheap, documented eating-disorder screen and escalation network embedded in GLP-1 telehealth intake.
customer: White-label medical groups that supply prescribers to many telehealth brands, GLP-1 telehealths, med spas and their malpractice carriers.
problem: GLP-1 use was ~50% among binge-eating-disorder patients and ~42% among atypical anorexia patients (JAMA Psychiatry 2026), and an NEJM 2026 perspective warned about masking and worsening disordered eating in telehealth. An investigation tied four white-label medical groups to ~30% of telehealth firms receiving FDA warning letters, and MDL 3094 has 4,700+ cases pending. Plaintiff lawyers and boards look for the next vector, and no screening or monitoring layer exists.
solution: A 3-minute validated screen (SCOFF or EDE-Q short form) inside intake, 2-question monthly check-ins, rules-based escalation to a network of ED-trained dietitians and therapists, and an exportable audit trail for boards and insurers.
why_now: FDA sent 30 letters in Mar 2026 and 25 in Jun 2026. Regulators, boards and carriers are moving to documented safeguards. The data showing high GLP-1 use in eating-disorder populations is new in 2026.
revenue_model: $3-6 per screened patient, $40-80 per escalation (paid by the prescriber or referral network), and a malpractice-carrier discount program.
non_obvious_insight: In white-label telehealth, liability concentrates in the medical group that sits behind dozens of brands, so a cheap, documented safeguard is standard-of-care insurance. ED providers also need referral flow, so escalation pays for itself.
first_30_days: Pitch two mid-size white-label groups or a 20k-patient telehealth. Deliver via an embeddable link, run 500 screens, and publish flag-rate benchmarks. Recruit 10 ED-trained clinicians for escalation.

title: Street-Level Gas Pipe Retirement Optimizer
one_liner: Software plus a turnkey block-by-block electrification crew that tells gas utilities which streets to retire instead of replace.
customer: Regulated gas distribution utilities in MA, NY, CO, MN, WA, CA and IL, and their regulators. Funding comes from pipe-replacement capex budgets.
problem: Electrification shrinks gas throughput, so fixed pipe costs land on fewer customers. Utilities still replace leak-prone mains at millions of dollars per mile. Regulators (for example Massachusetts DPU 20-80-B) demand non-pipeline alternatives, but nobody optimizes at street-segment level. Heat pump quotes run ~$9,000 and labor is scarce.
solution: GIS, billing and housing-stock analytics that score each pipe segment for retire-versus-replace, and find streets where electrifying 30-80 homes costs less than replacing the main. Then deliver the electrification block by block: group purchase, one crew per street per week, optionally networked geothermal. It is filed as a utility non-pipeline alternative.
why_now: State non-pipeline-alternative orders and thermal-energy-network laws are in force. With federal credits dead, utility-funded programs are the only scaled electrification channel. Ratepayer affordability pressure makes stranded pipe a live issue.
revenue_model: $250-500k a year SaaS per utility plus a per-home program fee ($5-12k) paid from avoided pipe capex.
non_obvious_insight: Gas utilities' problem is no longer selling heat pumps. It is stranded pipe. Their pipe replacement capex is the electrification budget hiding in plain sight.
first_30_days: Model one Massachusetts or New York utility territory from public leak-prone-pipe, assessor and census data. Publish a 'retire-first streets' list for one city. Pitch a city sustainability office, a regulator and two utility strategy VPs. Sell a $60-100k pilot analysis.

title: Robot Basecoating for Tabletop Miniature Armies
one_liner: A batch service where vision-guided robot airbrush cells prime, zenithal-shade and basecoat plastic miniatures so hobbyists only paint the details.
customer: Tabletop wargamers with unpainted backlogs, tournament players who need painted armies, and commission-painter studios who subcontract the tedious stages.
problem: An army is 100+ models, and priming and basecoating are the tedious first 60% of the work. Commission painters charge $10-60 per model and take months. Games Workshop's FY2026 revenue of GBP 626.8M shows the scale of the hobby.
solution: Customers ship assembled models. A low-cost robot arm learned from expert airbrushers primes, zenithal-shades and single-color basecoats. Humans QA and finish edges, and the army returns in about 10 days. Start human-in-the-loop with teleoperation and automate progressively.
why_now: Low-cost open-source robot arms and imitation-learning policies matured in 2025. A search for a commercial robot-airbrush painting service for miniatures found none.
revenue_model: $1.50-4 per model, $99-399 per army, and a subscription 'paint club' for batches.
non_obvious_insight: The community fetishizes painting but dislikes the first stage. The robot needs consistency, not artistry, on surfaces that hidden under detail work. Human painters keep the premium layer and become customers and distribution.
first_30_days: Hand-airbrush 50 armies to validate price and turnaround through r/Warhammer and local clubs. Build a teleop rig with a ~$3k arm and airbrush. Ship the first 20 orders.

title: Bereavement Aftercare for Independent Funeral Homes
one_liner: A white-label 13-month aftercare program that funeral homes buy to keep the newly widowed connected after the casseroles stop.
customer: Independent funeral homes (roughly 18,000 in the US, mostly independent), paying $200-350 per family served or a flat monthly fee.
problem: Grief tech money chases griefbots and digital memorials. The real gap is months 2-13, when widowhood drives isolation, depression and elevated mortality. Funeral directors hold the only list of newly bereaved households and a position of trust, but 'aftercare' is usually a brochure and a card. Cremation rates above 60% shrink revenue per call, and independents need loyalty and pre-need referrals to survive against consolidators.
solution: A packaged program: scheduled outreach calls at day 3, 14, 30 and 90, plus first-holiday and anniversary contacts. Small 'second-Thursday' peer groups hosted in the funeral home's own room. A paperwork concierge for Social Security, pensions and accounts, which is the logistics half of grief. A prolonged-grief screener at 6 months with referral to partner clinicians. Software runs scripts, scheduling, facilitator rosters and flags.
why_now: WHO's 2025 framing of loneliness as a measured global health metric gives directors a vocabulary and a reason to act. Rising cremation share squeezes revenue per family. Boomer-parent deaths are rising. Independents are hunting a differentiator against Service Corporation International-style chains.
revenue_model: $200-350 per family served billed to the funeral home, plus referral fees from partner therapists and an uplift in pre-need sales the home can attribute to the program.
non_obvious_insight: Griefbot founders sell to the bereaved at their worst moment. The natural customer for grief is the funeral director, who owns the list, is paid nothing after day 3, and buys aftercare as a marketing and retention expense at his best moment.
first_30_days: Sell 5 funeral homes at $300 per family through state funeral-director association meetings. Hire two part-time facilitators (hospice social workers). Run the first second-Thursday group. Track 6-month contact retention and pre-need referrals as the proof for the next 50 homes.

title: Sway Sensors for Liability Trees
one_liner: Clamp-on accelerometer nodes that learn each high-consequence tree's own sway signature and alert arborists when it changes, turning one-off tree risk assessments into a recurring monitored service.
customer: Owners of trees with large liability tails: campgrounds and RV parks, historic estates and cemeteries, school districts, HOAs, golf courses and city parks departments. Channel: consulting arborists with tree-risk qualifications, and public-entity insurers and risk pools.
problem: Tree risk assessment is a visual snapshot repeated every few years, yet storms and root decay can change risk overnight. Falling trees kill people in campgrounds and parks and generate large claims. Owners can't watch hundreds of trees, and arborists have no recurring revenue stream.
solution: A MEMS accelerometer and inclinometer node on the trunk (BOM in the tens of dollars) reporting sway frequency, damping and static tilt over LoRaWAN. Each tree is modeled against its own baseline plus local wind data. Anomalies such as a drop in natural frequency or new tilt trigger an arborist inspection within 24 hours. Annual reports combine the data with the arborist's assessment as a documented notice-and-response record. Deploy on the top 5-10% of trees over targets: tent pads, cabins, playgrounds.
why_now: Published work now supports the approach: LoRaWAN tree-tilt systems recorded failure modes during a super typhoon, and 2025-26 papers validate low-cost MEMS inclinometers and accelerometers for tree stability analysis. Cheap LoRaWAN gateways and stronger storm and drought volatility raise demand.
revenue_model: USD 8-15 per sensor per month plus a USD 99 hardware deposit. Arborist resellers keep about 30% and bill their own assessments. A 40-tree campground is about USD 6k per year. Insurer-funded programs for risk pools later.
non_obvious_insight: Don't try to predict failure. Trees differ, so each tree's own baseline is the model and change is the signal. The buyer's real purchase is documented reasonable care: proof of what they knew and when they acted. That also flips arborists from selling a triennial visual inspection to owning a recurring alert service.
first_30_days: Put off-the-shelf LoRa accelerometer nodes on 20 trees with two consulting arborists and one friendly campground or state park. Collect 90 days of sway data across a wind season. Partner with a university forestry program for validation and a publishable result. Sell the first pilot subscriptions to campgrounds at about USD 600 per year per site.

title: Launch-or-Rebook Guarantees for Rocket-Chasing Travelers
one_liner: A 'Launch Flex' add-on that hotels, charters and viewing events sell to fans, promising a rebook credit or refund if the target launch slips or scrubs, priced from launch history and weather.
customer: Space Coast and Starbase-area lodging, boat and viewing charters, ticketed viewing events and tour companies. Fans buy the add-on, and operators keep most of the premium.
problem: With 321 orbital launches in 2025 and Starship reaching orbit on 28 Sep 2026, launch-chasing has become a travel subculture. Dates slip and scrub, rates are non-refundable, and fans hesitate to commit. Operators either eat cancellations or lose bookings, and launch-night price spikes breed disputes.
solution: An embeddable add-on for operators' booking pages ($19-49). If the target launch slips beyond a defined window, the guest gets a rebook credit for the next launch or a partial refund. Risk is priced by vehicle, pad, provider and season from public launch logs and weather, starting as an operator-issued credit and later reinsured by a parametric MGA partner.
why_now: New vehicles and pads (Stoke's $1B raise, Starship orbital operations) add schedule variance and fans. Lead times are shrinking (37.5 to 33 days), and firm launch dates appear only days out. The launch-tourism audience is growing faster than operators' booking tools.
revenue_model: The platform keeps about 30% of the add-on premium, operators pay a $99 monthly widget fee, and later parametric-underwriting margin is added.
non_obvious_insight: A launch is a public, well-logged binary event with years of slip history, which makes travel risk easier to price than weather. Rebook credits let a hotel convert a demand spike into repeat visits instead of refunds.
first_30_days: Build a slip and scrub model from public launch logs. Sign 5 Titusville and Cocoa Beach hotels and 2 charter operators to pilot the add-on on their booking pages, and start collecting fees on the next 10 launches.

title: Regrade: Stamped Reclaimed Framing Lumber
one_liner: A mobile lumber re-grading and code-acceptance service that turns torn-out framing lumber from chip-pile waste into stamped, sellable studs and joists for ADUs, garages and additions.
customer: Deconstruction and demolition contractors and salvage yards (pay per board foot graded, or sell us stock). Small builders, ADU builders and remodelers buy packages.
problem: Framing costs are climbing (Austin framing up 25-50%, adding $2-5K per home, and builders estimate tariffs at about $10,900 per home). A 44-year median housing stock throws off tons of dimensional lumber, but yards cannot sell it for structural use because building officials want a grade stamp, so most of it is chipped for fuel or mulch at tens of dollars a ton.
solution: A truck-mounted setup with a certified grader, de-nailer and moisture scanner, working with an accredited grading agency or agency-approved third-party graders to re-grade and stamp. It also produces acceptance packets for local building departments. Sell 'ADU framing kits' and pre-nailed wall panels made from stamped reclaimed lumber at 20-35% below new.
why_now: Tariff-inflated lumber and a July 2026 ROAD to Housing Act that streamlines review for multifamily of 15 units or fewer and funds standard duplex/townhome plans should create a wave of small infill and ADU projects. Framing-crew scarcity also favors pre-made panels.
revenue_model: Grading fee per thousand board feet; margin on framing kits and panels; salvage purchases from deconstruction crews.
non_obvious_insight: The barrier to reuse is paper, not supply. Old true-dimension, slow-grown lumber often grades at or above new stock, and small builders' need for speed means the buyer will pay for panelization.
first_30_days: Confirm with an accredited grading agency and two local building departments what re-grade stamps and packets they accept. Hire a certified grader by the day. Contract 3 deconstruction crews for lumber. Sell one ADU frame or garage kit to prove code acceptance and margins.

title: Silver Crews: Retiree Work Co-ops for US Towns
one_liner: A membership co-op for retirees 62+ that contracts with towns, school districts and HOAs for short, insured, daytime jobs (crossing guards, school and library aides, grounds work, event staffing) and acts as employer of record.
customer: Municipal public-works and parks departments, school districts, libraries, HOAs and property managers who pay per job-hour. Retirees join as members.
problem: Employers with 5-15 hour-a-week daytime needs can't hire for them. Retirees want flexible, meaningful part-time work but distrust app gigs and can't easily get liability and accident cover. A record 4.18M Americans turned 65 in 2025, crossing guards are already the most senior-dominated occupation (nearly 1 in 3 are 65+), and about 15% of retirees say they'd consider returning to paid work.
solution: A county-level 'Silver Crew' modeled on Japan's Silver Human Resource Centers (about 1,300 centers, 700,000+ members). It recruits, background-checks and trains 200-400 members, holds standing contracts, schedules shifts, runs payroll (W-2 or contract), carries pooled workers'-comp/accident insurance, and hosts a monthly social meetup. Customers get a reliable pool without hiring headaches, and members get a community as well as a paycheck.
why_now: Peak 65 will stay elevated through at least 2027, school and municipal labor shortages persist, and municipal budgets favor contracting over adding headcount. Japan's centers have proven the model over decades, while US equivalents are small nonprofit senior-employment programs, not service-contract businesses.
revenue_model: Mark-up of roughly 15-25% on member pay billed to customers, small annual member dues, and margin on pooled insurance.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input isn't retiree labor, it's the wrapper. A town can't onboard a 68-year-old for six hours a week, but a co-op with pooled accident cover, one background-check process and a single invoice can. Japanese centers work because the arrangement is legally a contract for a task, not a job, which strips out friction. The social meetup is the retention engine, and it is what makes seniors choose this over Uber or DoorDash.
first_30_days: Pick one retiree-dense county (Florida, Arizona or a New England town). Sign 3 pilot contracts (an HOA, a school district and a library) using an existing PEO for payroll and workers' comp. Recruit 40 retirees through senior centers, churches and Nextdoor. Run the first paid shifts within 4 weeks and invoice monthly.

title: Pet-Safe Demand Response With Guaranteed Temperature Floors
one_liner: A demand-response layer that ties thermostat and battery dispatch to a cheap sensor where the pet actually lives, guaranteeing a temperature floor so pet owners stop opting out of grid flexibility.
customer: Co-op and municipal utilities and VPP/DR aggregators running thermostat or battery programs, who pay per enrolled and reliably-dispatched household. Pet insurers co-fund the sensors as a heatstroke-loss and brand play.
problem: Grid flexibility is now the scarce commodity (PJM's July auction cleared at the $325/MW-day cap and came up 6.8 GW short; the Duke study found 76 GW of new load could connect with 0.25% curtailment). Thermostat DR depends on enrollment and on people not overriding events, and events land on the hottest afternoons. Roughly 95M US households own a pet, and hypothesis to test in the first month: pets are a leading reason owners opt out or override, because an animal cannot consent to 82F. Aggregators treat that as unexplained churn and lost kW.
solution: Ship a $15-25 Wi-Fi temperature/humidity sensor placed in the pet zone, integrated as a hard constraint in the dispatch engine. The engine pre-cools earlier, caps setback by heat index, and auto-releases the event if the pet-zone sensor crosses the threshold. Owners get a visible 'pet-safe' program label, and the utility gets committed kW with lower override risk. Data is shared with the insurer only with consent.
why_now: Utilities and hyperscalers are buying 'firm' distributed capacity (Sunrun/Tesla/Renew Home's 16.8 GW capacity-as-a-service, with no disclosed verification standard), and 25C/25D ended 12/31/2025, shifting the economics toward utility-paid flexibility. Summer 2026 heat and record affordability pressure make participation and reliability the bottleneck.
revenue_model: Per-enrolled-household fee from utilities/aggregators ($10-30 per household per year), pilot fees ($25-40K), insurer co-funding of sensors, and later performance bonuses tied to reduced override rates.
non_obvious_insight: The most valuable DR customers are the ones who currently refuse because a living creature bears the risk. A sensor-backed guarantee converts a moral veto into a contract term, and pet insurers will subsidize it because heatstroke claims are avoidable. Verify the premise cheaply against override and opt-out data before building.
first_30_days: Pitch 5 distribution co-ops (there are hundreds) and one aggregator to add a pet-owner segment to an existing thermostat program. Survey opt-outs and pull override reasons. Hand-place 100 sensors and run one event with the pet-floor rule, comparing override rates against a control. Sell a $25-40K paid pilot with the results, and approach one pet insurer for sensor co-funding.

title: Whale-Proof Alert Network for Longline Boats
one_liner: A reciprocal, location-fuzzed alert network that lets sablefish and halibut longliners warn each other about orcas and sperm whales without giving up their fishing spots.
customer: Owner-operators of IFQ longline vessels in the Gulf of Alaska, Southeast and Bering Sea (roughly several hundred boats), sold through fishermen's associations, at $600-1,500 per vessel per season. Expansion buyers are pelagic longline fleets worldwide (tuna, toothfish) that also lose fish to whales.
problem: Whales strip the gear as it comes up, and bad sets lose a double-digit percentage of the catch. The whales learn the sound of your hauler and follow the boat, and sometimes the fleet. Every skipper knows it, but sightings travel only on private VHF codes and phone calls. Reporting a whale reveals where you are fishing. The boat that 'brings the whales' gets blamed. So the fleet's best early-warning data is never pooled.
solution: An app and text-message bot that runs over Garmin inReach, Iridium or Starlink. A skipper sends a one-line report ('killer whales, 8 mi of hall X'). The system publishes only a fuzzed geohash after a delay and strips vessel identity. You can see alerts only if you report (reciprocity credits). A model adds depredation-risk scores by area, soak time, season and haul timing. A playbook covers acoustic hygiene: hauler noise, set and haul timing, gear moves. An optional hydrophone kit comes later. Anonymized data goes to researchers, associations and insurers.
why_now: Quotas are tight and sablefish and halibut prices are well below their highs, so every whale-eaten pound matters more. Satellite texting from the wheelhouse is now cheap and near-universal (Starlink, inReach). Researchers have shown that whales learn from boat acoustics, which gives the fleet a reason to trust a shared system. Fishermen have also been moving toward pots to cope with whales, which shows they will pay for anything that works.
revenue_model: Per-vessel seasonal subscription ($600-1,500), association-level enterprise licenses, and anonymized depredation data sold to research programs, regulators and insurers. Upside is global pelagic longline fleets that all have the same depredation problem.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not detection technology, it is mechanism design. Skippers guard spots and fear blame, so they share whale sightings only in private. A network that gives value only to reporters, blurs location and time, and hides identity solves that. It is a game-theory product disguised as a whale app. Whale behavior is also fleet-learned, so tracking anonymized boat signatures over time is a data asset nobody else has.
first_30_days: Recruit 25 skippers in Sitka, Kodiak and Homer through the longline associations. The sablefish season closes mid-November, so use the winter to run it as a manual pilot: a group text plus a spreadsheet plus a simple map, paying $100 for reports. Interview skippers about how they signal each other today. Draft the fuzzing rules with them. Sell pre-season subscriptions in Feb-Mar and go live for the March opening.

title: Guardrail Gateway for Hotel AI Agents
one_liner: A proxy between hotel AI agents (voice, chat, booking) and PMS, POS and door-lock APIs that enforces per-action permissions, spend limits and human approval for irreversible actions.
customer: Hotel AI vendors that need enterprise trust, hotel groups' IT and security teams, and cyber insurers.
problem: Hotels are deploying agents fast (Dextr AI raised a USD 6.7M seed for hotel voice agents on 24 Sep 2026, and 109 AI use cases have been catalogued across 39 hotel systems). Practitioner commentary warns agents often hold API access built for trusted staff, so a prompt-injected guest message could trigger refunds, comps, rate changes or key issuance. PMS platforms have no concept of a scoped agent identity.
solution: An API and MCP gateway in front of PMS platforms (start with one that has a public API). It is read-only by default, applies caps on write actions (small refunds auto-approve, larger ones go to staff for approval in Slack or WhatsApp), redacts personal data, has a kill switch and keeps immutable logs. It ships with a red-team pack of injection attacks.
why_now: Agents are moving from pilots to production in 2026, PMS vendors are opening APIs, and agent protocols such as MCP are mainstream. Insurers and enterprise buyers are starting to ask for controls.
revenue_model: USD 49-149 per property per month, OEM licences to AI vendors, and insurer referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: In the agent gold rush the scarce item is the permission model, not the agent. AI vendors will pay for it as a sales enabler, and insurers will pay because it caps their loss.
first_30_days: Build against one PMS with a public API (Mews or Cloudbeds). Sign 2 hotel AI startups as design partners, and publish a red-team report showing injection weaknesses in demo agents (with permission) to earn press and inbound interest.

title: Home-Readiness Crews for Hospital-at-Home Programs
one_liner: On-call crews that make a patient's home hospital-ready in hours and provide a non-clinical overnight presence for the first 72 hours.
customer: Hospital-at-Home program directors at health systems, and Medicare Advantage plans and ACOs that fund them.
problem: Extending the waiver lets programs scale, but many referred patients get screened out because of clutter, stairs, pets, bad Wi-Fi or power, no bedside space, or no adult present overnight. Every screen-out is a lost admission that would have replaced $2,500+ inpatient days. No one owns the home itself.
solution: A van and two-person crew does a rapid home assessment (power, connectivity via hotspot or eSIM, safe path, bedside setup, hazard removal, DME handoff). A vetted sitter provides overnight presence and escalates to the nurse line, and the crew resets the home at discharge. An address-based readiness score pre-screens referrals before the ED sends them.
why_now: The Hospital-at-Home waiver was extended five years, to Sep 30, 2030, so systems are committing capital and hiring. 80+ growth and 90% occupancy in senior housing mean more frail patients whose homes are the constraint.
revenue_model: Per-episode fee of $350-900 plus monthly retainers for guaranteed response, and a software license for the readiness score.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource isn't clinicians or tech; it's a safe physical environment and a body in the room at 3 am. Whoever solves 'make the home hospital-grade' raises hospital-at-home conversion rates, which is what programs are judged on.
first_30_days: Pitch three hospital-at-home directors and offer a pilot at cost on 20 episodes, using existing local caregiver and sitter pools. Track screen-out conversion and cost per episode.

title: Smell Graders for Recycled Plastic
one_liner: A network of trained human noses that gives every batch of post-consumer recycled plastic an odor grade from 1 to 5, creating the price tier and spec that brands need to hit recycled-content mandates.
customer: Plastic recyclers selling PCR resin (HDPE, PP), converters that mold bottles and tubs, and brand owners in personal care, household and food buying PCR under EU and US recycled-content rules. The recyclers' quality managers buy first, then brand procurement teams.
problem: Odor is one of the biggest barriers to using recycled plastic. Recyclers can't tell buyers reliably what a batch smells like. Brands reject loads or cap PCR percentages out of caution. Lab methods such as GC-olfactometry are slow and costly, and there's no shared odor grade the way coffee has the Q-score.
solution: A standard protocol (heated headspace jars, blind triplicates, a reference odor kit, descriptor vocabulary such as rancid, detergent, smoky) run by a panel of trained sniffers recruited from perfumers, coffee Q-graders, sommeliers and food-sensory panelists. Recyclers mail samples and get a 48-hour graded report. Human scores then train an e-nose and GC model that lowers cost per test. Over time it becomes a certification: license and train graders, and publish the grade spec brands cite in purchase contracts.
why_now: The EU Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation applies from 12 August 2026, with 2030 recycled-content minimums (30% for contact-sensitive PET, 10% for other contact-sensitive plastics). Brands have to buy far more PCR within a few years. Sensor vendors need human-panel labels to train on, and none has a standard odor tier to price against.
revenue_model: $120 to $250 per batch grade. Weekly-lot subscriptions for recyclers. Vendor-qualification programs for brands at $30k or more per year. Grader certification and training fees. Licensing of the labeled dataset to e-nose makers.
non_obvious_insight: Regulation mandates recycled content, but a human nose decides whether the resin is usable, and buyers will not trust a grade until someone standardizes it. Whoever owns the grading standard sets the price tiers for the whole PCR market, a bit like coffee's Q-grading. Human panels remain the legal and commercial ground truth even after e-noses arrive.
first_30_days: Recruit 12 sniffers from local specialty roasters and perfume or flavor schools. Buy vials, a hot plate and a reference odor kit for under $1,000. Offer three regional recyclers free grading of 20 batches each, and check the grades against their buyers' rejection history. Then price it. Publish a free 'PCR smell atlas' to attract recycler and brand inbound.

title: Muscle Ultrasound Scans as a Gym Vital Sign
one_liner: A five-minute, AI-read thigh ultrasound that tells GLP-1 users and lifters whether they are keeping their muscle.
customer: Gyms, GLP-1 and weight-loss clinics and PT clinics; consumers pay $29-49 per scan, clinics pay per-scan licenses.
problem: Studies suggest 20-50 percent of weight lost on GLP-1 drugs can be lean mass, but scales, bioimpedance and photos cannot show muscle and DEXA is costly and inconvenient. Trainers and clinics have no cheap, objective muscle metric to motivate clients or steer dosing and training.
solution: A coach scans the quadriceps with a handheld probe; AI segments rectus femoris and vastus intermedius thickness and echogenicity; results are trended over time and against a cohort. Positioned as general wellness muscle-thickness tracking that integrates with training and nutrition plans, not diagnosis.
why_now: Handheld ultrasound now shows excellent agreement with cart systems for quadriceps thickness (ICC above 0.9 in a 2025 study), automated AI muscle segmentation is maturing, muscle loss on GLP-1s was a headline debate at ADA 2026, and the FDA's wellness posture is looser.
revenue_model: $29-49 per scan retail; gym device-plus-software rental at $299-499 per month; per-scan fees for clinics.
non_obvious_insight: Trend in thickness, not absolute mass, is precise enough to change behavior. It is a retention and upsell tool for gyms (more strength coaching for people who can see the muscle they are protecting).
first_30_days: Buy two handheld probes, validate against DEXA on 50 volunteers with a partner clinic, run scan days at three gyms and one GLP-1 clinic at $39 per scan, and sign the first monthly device subscription.

title: Medicaid Hours Wallet for Gig Workers
one_liner: A phone-based monthly proof-of-work ledger that turns gig, cash and self-employment activity into state-accepted documentation and 30-day cure packets, paid for by the Medicaid plans and health centers that lose revenue when members drop.
customer: Medicaid managed care organizations with expansion-adult lines, and FQHC and community health center networks. Medicaid is 43-50% of health center revenue, and an MCO is paid capitation per member-month. End users are expansion adults aged 19-64 with irregular income. The MCO or health center pays per retained member; the enrollee pays nothing.
problem: CMS's interim final rule (June 3, 2026) requires states to implement 80 hours a month of work or activity, or $580 a month in income, by Jan 1, 2027. Compliance is checked at application and at renewal, and a noncompliance notice gives 30 calendar days to cure. CBO projects about 4.8M coverage losses from work requirements, largely from reporting complexity. About 9 in 10 affected patients are expected to qualify for an exemption or already comply, yet many will still lose coverage on documentation. Nebraska went live May 1, 2026 with self-attestation, but about 28,000 people there must document twice a year and the state plans to move to verification.
solution: An enrollee-side SMS and app tool. It ingests bank and payment-app statements, gig platform earnings exports (Uber, DoorDash, Cash App, Venmo), pay stub photos and logged volunteer or class hours. It computes whether each month clears $580 or 80 hours and generates the state-specific verification packet. It sends look-back-month reminders and prepares the 30-day cure response. It flags likely exemption candidates, such as medically frail members, from plan claims data. The plan or clinic dashboard shows at-risk members and cure success. The tool only assists and never determines compliance, which is what federal rules allow plans to do.
why_now: The interim final rule was published June 3, 2026, and the national start date is Jan 1, 2027. Nebraska's live rollout is the preview of what other states will face when verification replaces self-attestation. CMS is encouraging automation, but states are spending on caseworker portals, notices and screening tools, not on income documentation for gig workers.
revenue_model: $3-8 per at-risk member per month billed to the MCO, or a success fee of $50-150 per member retained through renewal. FQHC SaaS at $2-5k per month per site with an outcomes dashboard. Later, state contracts for a self-employed and gig documentation module.
non_obvious_insight: Vendors such as Salesforce are building state-facing portals for applicants and caseworkers. The parties with a P&L at stake, the MCOs and health centers, are not yet being sold a member-side tool. KFF's roundup of state outreach plans covers notices, websites and screening tools but does not describe how self-employed or irregular income will be documented (https://www.kff.org/medicaid/medicaid-work-requirements-federal-outreach-requirements-and-state-plans/). State wage-data matching misses 1099, cash and gig work by design. Georgetown's CCF warns that 'verification in this context means burdensome documentation requirements for enrollees' (https://ccf.georgetown.edu/2026/05/11/the-new-medicaid-work-reporting-requirements-are-here-dont-let-the-nebraska-soft-start-fool-you/). The retention math is lopsided: a plan or clinic can pay a few dollars a month per member to protect several hundred dollars of monthly revenue. Sources: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/06/03/2026-11094/medicaid-program-community-engagement-requirement-for-certain-individuals and https://www.pointcare.com/blog/how-to-prevent-medicaid-coverage-gaps-in-2026
first_30_days: Build the Nebraska flow first, since it is already live. Recruit 50 gig and self-employed Medicaid enrollees through one FQHC partner. Measure how many can produce a compliant $580 or 80-hour packet within 30 days. Take those results to two MCO member-engagement and quality leads for a paid pilot. Sign an LOI with one health center network before Jan 1, 2027.
